convolution.name: convolution
convolution.definition: A shared local weighted sum applied across spatial positions.
convolution.explanation: In neural-network libraries, convolution usually means cross-correlation: the kernel is not flipped before multiplication. A small kernel visits every image position, reusing the same weights, so it can detect a pattern wherever that pattern appears. Local connectivity preserves spatial structure and weight sharing limits the parameter count. A convolution layer may have several learned filters, each producing one output channel. Padding and stride determine which positions are visited and therefore the output shape.

padding.name: padding
padding.definition: Extra values conceptually placed around an input before a spatial operation.
padding.explanation: Zero padding lets a kernel be centered near an image boundary even though part of its window falls outside the stored pixels. The missing positions contribute zero. With a 3×3 kernel, stride one, and one pixel of padding, output height and width equal the input dimensions. Padding is an architectural choice, not additional observed data. Different padding policies change boundary behavior and must be applied consistently in the forward and backward passes.

stride.name: stride
stride.definition: The number of input positions moved between neighboring kernel applications.
stride.explanation: Stride one evaluates every adjacent location. Stride two skips every other position and usually reduces spatial resolution. For input size I, kernel size K, padding P, and stride S, the output size is floor((I + 2P − K)/S) + 1 when the numerator is nonnegative. Stride changes both computation and which details are retained. It should not be confused with the memory stride used to index a row-major array.

pooling.name: pooling
pooling.definition: A fixed reduction over a small spatial neighborhood.
pooling.explanation: Max pooling keeps the largest activation in each window, while average pooling keeps the mean. Pooling reduces spatial size and makes later layers less sensitive to small local shifts. In backpropagation, average pooling distributes a gradient across every input; max pooling routes it only to the recorded winning position. Exact ties make max pooling nondifferentiable, so gradient checks should use inputs with a unique winner in every tested window.

receptive-field.name: receptive field
receptive-field.definition: The input region that can influence a particular activation.
receptive-field.explanation: One 3×3 convolutional activation sees a 3×3 image patch. Deeper stacks combine nearby activations, so their effective receptive fields grow even when every kernel remains small. Pooling and stride make the field grow faster by reducing spatial resolution. Receptive field describes possible influence, not proof that every pixel contributes equally after training. It helps connect architecture choices to the scale of patterns a network can represent.
